They determine it via two comparisons of training effort: layer depth and convergence speed.

They compare training effort from two perspectives — the number of layers and the convergence speed of the encoder and decoder [10]. For depth, they vary the number of encoder and decoder layers respectively, reasoning that deeper components yielding more gains indicate a task needing more representation capability and thus harder to learn; adding more encoder layers achieves larger improvements than adding more decoder layers [9][2]. For convergence, they fix the parameters of a well-trained decoder (encoder), update only the encoder (decoder), and find the decoder converges faster than the encoder [2][7]. From these two results — more gains from deeper encoder layers and the encoder needing more training time — they conclude the encoder handles a more difficult task than the decoder, i.e., the decoder's task is easier [8].

3 Hard for Encoder, Easy for Decoder In general, the encoder and decoder perform dif- ferent functionalities in an NMT model. In this section, we compare the characteristics between the encoder and decoder by analyzing the dif- ﬁculty of the corresponding task they handle in NMT. We investigate the task difﬁculty by com- paring the training effort of the encoder and de- coder from two perspectives: the number of layers and the convergence speed for the encoder and de- coder respectively.

1) We ﬁnd that adding more layers to the encoder achieves larger improvements than adding more layers to the decoder. 2) We also compare the training time of the en- coder and decoder by ﬁxing the parameters of a well-trained decoder (encoder), and just up- date the parameters of the encoder (decoder). We found that the decoder converges faster than the encoder. These two results suggest that the decoder handles an easier task than the encoder in NMT.
